canonical.name: Every density and translation theorem on this page keeps the hypothesis $1 \le p < \infty$ explicit; the $L^\infty$ side is handled instead by the exact closure theorem and the nonseparability witness.
The Euclidean $C_c$-density proof uses an explicit distance-function cutoff rather than the general Urysohn lemma as a load-bearing dependency.
The general separability theorem is stated only for sigma-finite measures on countably generated sigma-algebras, matching the published hypothesis ledger and not the false unrestricted slogan.
Convolution is defined through Borel representatives; arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable representatives can fail measurability after composition with the subtraction map.
Minkowski's integral inequality uses only the explicit dual norming vector and does not cite MT-16 or Hahn-Banach.
No new bump lemma is introduced on this page; the published smooth compactly supported bump is the seed of the mollifier family.
The page fixes the translation convention as $(\tau_h f)(x)=f(x-h)$ so the later continuity and convolution formulas use one sign convention.
The Euclidean spaces $C_c(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ provide the compact-support and mollifier vocabulary for the density route.
Convolution is recorded as $f*g(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x-y)g(y)\,dy$, with the representative discipline made explicit later on the page.
Finite-measure measurable sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ can be approximated in measure by finite unions of boxes, which is the regularity step behind box-step density.
Finite linear combinations of box indicators are dense in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for $1 \le p < \infty$.
Finite-measure measurable sets admit compact-open sandwiches with arbitrarily small excess, which is the local regularity input for $C_c$ density.
A countable generator yields a countable algebra of sets after closing under the finite Boolean operations used in the separability proof.
Finite-measure sets are approximable in symmetric-difference measure by sets from a countable generating algebra.
Compactly supported continuous functions are translation-continuous in $L^p$, providing the dense-subclass step in the general translation theorem.
Convolution on $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is bilinear, commutative, and associative once the almost-everywhere existence theorem is in place.
The support of a convolution lies in the closure of the Minkowski sum of the supports.
For conjugate exponents, convolution lands in $C_0(\mathbb{R}^n)$: it is continuous and vanishes at infinity.
A unit-mass smooth bump generates an $L^1$ approximate identity under the page's normalization.
Convolution with a mollifier is smooth, and derivatives pass under the integral sign.
